A vacuum tube is a device that allows electric current to pass through a vacuum. Through the "Edison effect", electrons flow from the cathode to the anode within the tube. By adding a grid, it can become a vacuum triode. Vacuum tubes have been widely used in radio, telephone, television, radar, and early computers.

For centuries, farmers sowed grain by hand, walking and burying seeds in the soil or scattering them broadly. The problem with this method was that seeds were not evenly distributed, so most were wasted. Jethro Tull invented a horse-drawn seed drill that used a box to hold seeds and a reed to scatter them. As the animal walked across the field, seeds were evenly scattered into the soil.

The Rotherham plough, also known as the Yorkshire plough, was improved by Disney and Joseph from a Dutch "fashion" plough. It used wood to secure all parts: the ploughshare, shovel, and board... It was lighter than traditional ploughs and more suitable for animal traction.

A telephone switchboard is a system composed of electrical components used to connect telephones. The telecommunications switchboard was invented in 1877 by a Hungarian working for Edison. In 1881, telephone switchboards were first used for commercial purposes on the US East Coast and Western Europe. Switchboards included hundreds of slots where employees manually plugged and unplugged lines to connect callers. In 1891, Almon Brown patented the automatic telephone switchboard.
